children: AS ROBOTS GET SMARTER, UBS POSITIONS FOR THE SUPPLIERS

Artificial intelligence is moving from screens into the physical world of factories, warehouses and hospitals, creating opportunities for the companies supplying the hardware behind the next generation of autonomous machines.

UBS Wealth Management argues that in-context learning is accelerating the shift to "physical AI". Instead of relying on a long training cycle, robots can now learn new tasks after watching a human perform them just a handful of times.
"We have officially entered the era of physical AI," says Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, UBS Wealth Management's CIO for the Americas and Global Head of Equities.
For investors, UBS says the most attractive opportunities may lie with the firms supplying critical components.
The bank highlights three key parts of the supply chain.
First are the precision gears and actuators that allow bots to move accurately, a market where manufacturing capacity is heavily concentrated among a few specialist firms globally.

Second are sensors such as LiDAR and cameras that help machines interpret their surroundings, with companies developing electronic skin and high-frequency optical sensors seen as particularly well positioned.
Third are specialised chips, computing hardware and batteries needed to process information and operate efficiently.
"We believe that the companies making the gears that move humanoid robots, the sensors that let them see, and the chips that let them think will become more valuable over time," she says.
